Direct-Current Circuits

Kirchhoff's rules, networks & RC transients

27.0 — Reading the Circuit

Chapter 26 ended with two wires joined end to end — a metre of nichrome and ten metres of copper across one battery. Two rules settled it: the pieces carry one current, so their voltages add. That pair of wires was already a circuit. This chapter takes the same two rules and applies them to networks of any shape.

A single battery and a single resistor is the simplest circuit there is. Real devices — a phone, a car’s electrical system, the power grid — are networks of elements that cannot be reduced by inspection alone. The tools for them come from Gustav Robert Kirchhoff (1824–1887), who in 1845, as a 21-year-old student at the University of Königsberg, published two rules that formalize what we already know about charge and energy. His junction rule says charge cannot pile up at a node; his loop rule says potential is single-valued. Together they reduce any circuit, however complex, to a system of linear equations.

“The algebraic sum of the currents at any junction point is zero; the algebraic sum of the potential differences around any closed loop is zero.” — Gustav Kirchhoff, 1845

Real batteries, series and parallel combinations, multi-battery networks and RC circuits all yield to the same two rules. The chapter closes a loop opened in Chapter 25: where the “missing” half of the energy goes when a capacitor charges.

*Personal note: Kirchhoff was 21 when he published these rules. They remain, nearly two centuries later, the foundation of every circuit analysis course in the world. Simplicity, when it captures the right physics, is timeless.

27.1 — EMF and Internal Resistance

The Electromotive Force

Chapter 26 treated a battery as an ideal source of constant potential difference. The electromotive force (EMF), \(\mathcal{E}\), is the energy the battery gives each unit of charge that passes through it — the potential difference it maintains when no current flows. Despite its name, EMF is not a force; it is a voltage, measured in volts. The name is older than the distinction between force and energy.

Real Batteries and Terminal Voltage

A real battery has internal resistance \(r\) — the resistance of the chemicals and electrodes the current must pass through. We model it as an ideal EMF \(\mathcal{E}\) in series with \(r\), connected to an external load \(R\):

Step 1 — the energy supplied. Each coulomb that passes through the battery gains energy \(\mathcal{E}\) (Chapter 24: a potential difference is energy per unit charge).

Step 2 — one current. The battery’s interior and the load are in one unbroken path, so by Chapter 26 they carry the same current \(I\).

Step 3 — the drops add. The coulomb gives up \(Ir\) inside the battery and \(IR\) in the load — the two-wires-end-to-end result of Chapter 26. It returns to where it started, so the energy gained equals the energy given up:

\[\mathcal{E} = Ir + IR\]

Step 4 — solve.

\[\boxed{\;I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R + r}\;}\]

The terminal voltage — what a voltmeter across the battery’s terminals reads — is the drop across the load, \(IR\):

\[\boxed{\;\Delta V_\text{term} = \mathcal{E} - Ir\;}\]

Check the limits.

  • Open circuit (\(R \to \infty\)). \(I \to 0\), so \(\Delta V_\text{term} \to \mathcal{E}\). With no current there is no drop inside the battery — which is why the EMF is defined at zero current.
  • Short circuit (\(R \to 0\)). \(I \to \mathcal{E}/r\), finite, and \(\Delta V_\text{term} \to 0\). A real battery cannot deliver infinite current, and all its power is dissipated inside it as heat. This is why short circuits are dangerous.
  • Ideal battery (\(r \to 0\)). \(\Delta V_\text{term} = \mathcal{E}\) at every current — the Chapter 26 model, recovered.

The Power Budget

Multiply Step 3 by \(I\):

\[I\mathcal{E} = I^2R + I^2r\]

The left side is the power the EMF delivers; the right side is where it goes — into the load and into the battery itself. This is Chapter 26’s \(P = I^2R\), applied to both resistances that share the current.

The compressed-air canister. The canister’s internal pressure plays the EMF — the most driving pressure available. The nozzle is the load: a narrow nozzle (large \(R\)) lets little air out and holds the outlet near full pressure. Open it wider (smaller \(R\)) and more air flows, but the outlet pressure drops, because more of the canister’s pressure is spent pushing air through its own internal passages (the internal resistance \(r\)). Fully open (\(R \to 0\)), the flow is as large as the canister can sustain and the outlet pressure is zero — the short circuit.

Property Ideal battery Real battery
Internal resistance \(r = 0\) \(r > 0\)
Terminal voltage \(\Delta V = \mathcal{E}\) \(\Delta V = \mathcal{E} - Ir\)
Power to load \(P = \mathcal{E}I\) \(P = \mathcal{E}I - I^2r\)
Short-circuit current \(\infty\) \(\mathcal{E}/r\)

Example: Terminal Voltage Under Load, and an Aging Battery

A battery has \(\mathcal{E} = 12.0\) V and \(r = 0.050\ \Omega\). It is connected to a load \(R = 3.00\ \Omega\).

Step 1 — the current.

\[I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R + r} = \frac{12.0}{3.00 + 0.050} = 3.93\ \text{A}\]

Step 2 — the terminal voltage.

\[\boxed{\;\Delta V_\text{term} = 12.0 - (3.93)(0.050) = 11.8\ \text{V}\;}\]

Step 3 — the power budget. To the load, \(I^2R = 46.4\) W; inside the battery, \(I^2r = 0.77\) W. The battery delivers 98% of its power to the load.

Step 4 — the same battery, aged. Its EMF barely changes, but \(r\) rises to \(2.00\ \Omega\). Now \(I = 12.0/5.00 = 2.40\) A, the terminal voltage falls to \(12.0 - (2.40)(2.00) = 7.2\) V, and the internal loss is \(I^2r = 11.5\) W — 40% of the \(28.8\) W the EMF delivers.

Check the budget. Aged: \(I^2R + I^2r = (2.40)^2(3.00) + 11.5 = 17.3 + 11.5 = 28.8\) W \(= I\mathcal{E}\). An old battery “dies” not because its EMF is gone — a voltmeter on the bench still reads nearly 12 V — but because its internal resistance eats the terminal voltage as soon as a current is drawn.

*Personal note: This is why car batteries feel warm after cranking a starter motor. The starter draws hundreds of amps, and \(I^2r\) losses are substantial.

27.2 — Resistors in Series and Parallel

Chapter 25 combined capacitors by asking one question: what do the pieces share? Resistors are combined the same way.

Series Combination

Resistors connected end to end, with no branch between them, are in series:

Step 1 — what is shared. There is one path, so every resistor carries the same current \(I\) (Chapter 26).

Step 2 — the drops add. A charge crossing all three gives up energy in each: \(\Delta V = \Delta V_1 + \Delta V_2 + \Delta V_3\).

Step 3 — substitute \(\Delta V_i = IR_i\). \(\Delta V = I(R_1 + R_2 + R_3)\). A single resistor that draws the same \(I\) from the same \(\Delta V\) is the equivalent resistance:

\[\boxed{\;R_\text{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \cdots \qquad \text{(series)}\;}\]

Parallel Combination

Resistors connected across the same two nodes are in parallel:

Step 1 — what is shared. Each resistor connects the same two nodes, and potential has one value at a node (Chapter 24), so every resistor has the same \(\Delta V\).

Step 2 — the currents add. Charge cannot pile up where the branches split, so the current in equals the currents out: \(I = I_1 + I_2 + I_3\).

Step 3 — substitute \(I_i = \Delta V/R_i\). \(I = \Delta V\,(1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3)\), and \(I = \Delta V/R_\text{eq}\):

\[\boxed{\;\frac{1}{R_\text{eq}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3} + \cdots \qquad \text{(parallel)}\;}\]

For two resistors, \(R_\text{eq} = R_1R_2/(R_1 + R_2)\).

Check the limits.

  • Series is larger than the largest. Every term is positive, so adding a resistor in series can only raise \(R_\text{eq}\). Adding \(R \to 0\) (a wire) changes nothing.
  • Parallel is smaller than the smallest. Each branch is another path; adding one can only lower \(R_\text{eq}\). A branch with \(R \to \infty\) (an open switch) changes nothing; a branch with \(R \to 0\) shorts the whole combination to \(R_\text{eq} \to 0\).
  • Two equal resistors. Series gives \(2R\); parallel gives \(R/2\) — twice the length, or twice the area, exactly as \(R = \rho\ell/A\) predicts.

Capacitors and resistors combine in reverse.

Property Capacitors (Ch 25) Resistors (Ch 27)
Defining equation \(C = Q/\Delta V\) \(R = \Delta V/I\)
Geometry \(C = \varepsilon_0A/d\) \(R = \rho\ell/A\)
Larger area → larger \(C\) smaller \(R\)
Shared in series charge \(Q\) current \(I\)
Shared in parallel voltage \(\Delta V\) voltage \(\Delta V\)
Series rule \(1/C_\text{eq} = \sum 1/C_i\) \(R_\text{eq} = \sum R_i\)
Parallel rule \(C_\text{eq} = \sum C_i\) \(1/R_\text{eq} = \sum 1/R_i\)

Why reversed? In series, both share the flowing quantity (\(Q\) or \(I\)) and their voltages add. For a resistor \(\Delta V = IR\) puts \(R\) in the numerator, so the \(R\)’s add; for a capacitor \(\Delta V = Q/C\) puts \(C\) in the denominator, so the \(1/C\)’s add. The same question — what is shared? — gives opposite rules because the defining equations are built the opposite way round.

Example: A Mixed Resistor Network

\(R_1 = 8.0\ \Omega\) and \(R_2 = 4.0\ \Omega\) are in series. \(R_3 = 6.0\ \Omega\) and \(R_4 = 3.0\ \Omega\) are in parallel. The two sub-networks are connected in series across \(\Delta V = 42\) V.

Step 1 — reduce the series pair. \(R_{12} = 8.0 + 4.0 = 12.0\ \Omega\).

Step 2 — reduce the parallel pair. \(R_{34} = (6.0)(3.0)/(6.0 + 3.0) = 2.0\ \Omega\).

Step 3 — the whole network. \(R_{12}\) and \(R_{34}\) share one current, so they add:

\[\boxed{\;R_\text{eq} = 12.0 + 2.0 = 14.0\ \Omega, \qquad I = \frac{42}{14.0} = 3.0\ \text{A}\;}\]

Step 4 — work back out. The parallel pair has \(\Delta V_{34} = (3.0)(2.0) = 6.0\) V across each branch, so \(I_3 = 6.0/6.0 = 1.0\) A and \(I_4 = 6.0/3.0 = 2.0\) A.

Check it two ways. The currents add at the junction: \(1.0 + 2.0 = 3.0\) A. The power adds too: \((3.0)^2(8.0) + (3.0)^2(4.0) + (1.0)^2(6.0) + (2.0)^2(3.0) = 72 + 36 + 6 + 12 = 126\) W, and \(I\Delta V = (3.0)(42) = 126\) W.

27.3 — Kirchhoff’s Rules

When Series and Parallel Aren’t Enough

Many circuits cannot be reduced to series and parallel pieces. With two batteries in different branches, no pair of resistors shares a current and no pair shares a voltage; one battery may even drive current backwards through the other. Kirchhoff’s two rules handle every case.

The Junction Rule

At any junction,

\[\boxed{\;\sum I_\text{in} = \sum I_\text{out}\;}\]

This is charge conservation — Chapter 26’s “one current along the whole wire”, applied where the wire branches. In a steady state no charge piles up at a node.

The Loop Rule

Around any closed loop,

\[\boxed{\;\sum \Delta V = 0\;}\]

This is Chapter 24’s statement that potential is single-valued: walk around any closed path and return to the start, and you are back at the same potential. In energy terms, a charge that goes around a loop gains in the batteries exactly what it gives up in the resistors — the same accounting as Step 3 of §27.1.

Sign Conventions

Element traversed Direction \(\Delta V\)
Resistor \(R\) with the assumed current \(I\) \(-IR\)
Resistor \(R\) against the assumed current \(I\) \(+IR\)
EMF \(\mathcal{E}\) from \(-\) to \(+\) \(+\mathcal{E}\)
EMF \(\mathcal{E}\) from \(+\) to \(-\) \(-\mathcal{E}\)

The sign convention is bookkeeping, not physics. Assume any direction for each current. If an assumption is wrong, the algebra returns a negative value — which means only that the current flows the other way.

Problem-Solving Strategy

  1. Label each branch current with an assumed direction.
  2. Apply the junction rule. \(J\) junctions give \(J - 1\) independent equations.
  3. Apply the loop rule to independent loops. With \(B\) branches you need \(B - (J - 1)\) loop equations — one per unknown left over.
  4. Solve, then verify with a loop you did not use.

*Personal note: Kirchhoff’s rules reduce circuit analysis to linear algebra. The skill is in choosing convenient junctions and loops, not in the physics itself. The physics is just charge conservation and energy conservation.

Example: A Strong Battery Charging a Weak One

\(\mathcal{E}_1 = 6.0\) V, \(\mathcal{E}_2 = 12.0\) V, \(R_1 = 2.0\ \Omega\), \(R_2 = 2.0\ \Omega\), \(R_3 = 8.0\ \Omega\), connected as shown. Find the current in each branch.

Step 1 — the junction rule at B.

\[I_1 = I_2 + I_3 \qquad \text{(Eq. 1)}\]

Step 2 — loop 1 (D → A → B → E → D, clockwise). Up through \(\mathcal{E}_1\) from \(-\) to \(+\), then with \(I_1\) through \(R_1\), then with \(I_3\) down through \(R_3\):

\[+6.0 - 2.0\,I_1 - 8.0\,I_3 = 0 \qquad \text{(Eq. 2)}\]

Step 3 — loop 2 (E → B → C → F → E). Up through \(R_3\) against \(I_3\), then with \(I_2\) through \(R_2\), then down through \(\mathcal{E}_2\) from \(+\) to \(-\):

\[+8.0\,I_3 - 2.0\,I_2 - 12.0 = 0 \qquad \text{(Eq. 3)}\]

Step 4 — solve. Eq. 2 gives \(I_1 = 3.0 - 4.0\,I_3\); Eq. 3 gives \(I_2 = 4.0\,I_3 - 6.0\). Substituting both into Eq. 1: \(3.0 - 4.0\,I_3 = 5.0\,I_3 - 6.0\), so \(I_3 = 1.0\) A.

\[\boxed{\;I_1 = -1.0\ \text{A}, \qquad I_2 = -2.0\ \text{A}, \qquad I_3 = 1.0\ \text{A}\;}\]

Step 5 — read the signs. \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) came out negative, so both flow opposite to the arrows. The 12 V battery drives 2.0 A out of its \(+\) terminal, toward B. There the current splits: 1.0 A down through \(R_3\), and 1.0 A backwards through \(R_1\) into the \(+\) terminal of the 6 V battery — the strong battery is charging the weak one.

Check with the loop we did not use (D → A → B → C → F → D): \(+6.0 - (-1.0)(2.0) - (-2.0)(2.0) - 12.0 = 6.0 + 2.0 + 4.0 - 12.0 = 0\). ✓

Check the power. The 12 V battery delivers \((2.0)(12.0) = 24\) W. It goes to \(R_1\), \(R_2\), \(R_3\) — \(2.0 + 8.0 + 8.0 = 18\) W — and 6.0 W into the 6 V battery, stored as chemical energy. Total: 24 W. ✓

A terminal voltage larger than the EMF. Suppose \(R_1\) is the weak battery’s own internal resistance. Its terminal voltage is the potential of B above E: \(\Delta V_{BE} = I_3R_3 = 8.0\) V — more than its 6.0 V EMF. §27.1’s \(\Delta V_\text{term} = \mathcal{E} - Ir\) still holds; the current now flows backwards through the battery, so \(I\) is negative and the “drop” across \(r\) adds: \(6.0 - (-1.0)(2.0) = 8.0\) V. This is what charging looks like, and it is how a jump-start works.

27.4 — RC Circuits: Charging and Discharging

A New Kind of Circuit

Every circuit so far has been in a steady state, with currents constant in time. Put a resistor and a capacitor in the same loop and something new happens: the current changes with time. The resistor limits how fast charge can reach the capacitor, and the capacitor’s growing voltage pushes back, producing an exponential approach to equilibrium.

Charging

An uncharged capacitor \(C\) is in series with a resistor \(R\) and a battery \(\mathcal{E}\). At \(t = 0\) the switch closes.

Step 1 — the loop rule at time \(t\). With charge \(q\) on the capacitor and current \(I\) in the loop, the capacitor’s voltage is \(q/C\) (Chapter 25):

\[\mathcal{E} - IR - \frac{q}{C} = 0\]

Step 2 — the bridging step: \(I = dq/dt\). The current in the loop is the rate at which charge arrives on the capacitor plate. This is the step that turns a loop equation into a differential equation in one unknown, \(q(t)\).

\[R\,\frac{dq}{dt} = \mathcal{E} - \frac{q}{C} = \frac{C\mathcal{E} - q}{C}\]

Step 3 — separate the variables.

\[\frac{dq}{C\mathcal{E} - q} = \frac{dt}{RC}\]

Step 4 — integrate from \(q = 0\) at \(t = 0\) to \(q\) at \(t\):

\[-\ln\!\left(\frac{C\mathcal{E} - q}{C\mathcal{E}}\right) = \frac{t}{RC} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad C\mathcal{E} - q = C\mathcal{E}\,e^{-t/RC}\]

Step 5 — solve for \(q\), then differentiate for \(I\). Writing \(Q_\text{max} = C\mathcal{E}\) and \(I_0 = \mathcal{E}/R\):

\[\boxed{\;q(t) = Q_\text{max}\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right), \qquad I(t) = \frac{dq}{dt} = I_0\,e^{-t/RC}\;}\]

Check the limits.

  • At \(t = 0\): \(q = 0\), so the capacitor has no voltage and \(I = \mathcal{E}/R\) — the whole EMF is across the resistor. An uncharged capacitor acts like a wire.
  • As \(t \to \infty\): \(q \to C\mathcal{E}\) and \(I \to 0\) — the capacitor’s voltage matches the battery’s and nothing flows. A full capacitor acts like an open switch.
  • Larger \(R\) or larger \(C\) means slower. Larger \(R\) limits the current; larger \(C\) needs more charge to reach the same voltage. Both lengthen the climb.

Discharging

Now the capacitor starts with charge \(Q_0\) and is connected across \(R\) alone. The loop rule is \(q/C - IR = 0\), but the plate is losing charge, so the current that flows is \(I = -dq/dt\):

\[\frac{dq}{dt} = -\frac{q}{RC} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{dq}{q} = -\frac{dt}{RC}\]

Integrating from \(Q_0\) at \(t = 0\):

\[\boxed{\;q(t) = Q_0\,e^{-t/RC}, \qquad I(t) = \frac{Q_0}{RC}\,e^{-t/RC}\;}\]

The current flows out of the positive plate, opposite to the charging current. \(Q_0\) is whatever charge the capacitor holds when discharge begins — \(C\mathcal{E}\) if it was fully charged, less if charging was interrupted.

The Time Constant

\[\boxed{\;\tau = RC\;}\]

*Personal note: The dimensional analysis is worth doing explicitly: \([\Omega][\text{F}] = (\text{V/A})(\text{C/V}) = \text{C/A} = \text{s}\). Resistance slows the flow; capacitance sets how much charge must flow. Their product is a time.

Time Charging: \(q/Q_\text{max}\) Discharging: \(q/Q_0\)
\(t = \tau\) 63.2% 36.8%
\(t = 2\tau\) 86.5% 13.5%
\(t = 3\tau\) 95.0% 5.0%
\(t = 5\tau\) 99.3% 0.7%

The table answers “how full after a given time.” The reverse question — how long to reach a given fraction — needs the exponential inverted with a logarithm.

Example: An RC Circuit, Forwards and Backwards

\(R = 8.00 \times 10^5\ \Omega\), \(C = 5.00\ \mu\)F, \(\mathcal{E} = 12.0\) V.

Step 1 — the scales.

\[\tau = RC = (8.00 \times 10^5)(5.00 \times 10^{-6}) = 4.00\ \text{s}, \qquad Q_\text{max} = C\mathcal{E} = 60.0\ \mu\text{C}, \qquad I_0 = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R} = 15.0\ \mu\text{A}\]

Step 2 — forwards: the state at \(t = \tau\). \(q = 60.0(1 - e^{-1}) = 37.9\ \mu\)C and \(I = 15.0\,e^{-1} = 5.52\ \mu\)A.

Step 3 — backwards: how long to reach 90%? Set \(q/Q_\text{max} = 1 - e^{-t/\tau} = 0.900\), so \(e^{-t/\tau} = 0.100\). Take the natural log of both sides:

\[-\frac{t}{\tau} = \ln(0.100) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad t = \tau\ln 10\]

\[\boxed{\;t = 2.30\,\tau = 9.21\ \text{s}\;}\]

Check against the table. \(2.30\tau\) sits between \(2\tau\) (86.5%) and \(3\tau\) (95.0%), as 90% should. And the discharge mirror: dropping to 10% of \(Q_0\) means \(e^{-t/\tau} = 0.100\) — the same equation, so the same \(t = 2.30\tau\). Charging to 90% and discharging to 10% take the same time.

Energy in RC Charging: The 50% Result

Chapter 25 left a loose end: when a charged capacitor shares its charge with an empty one, half the energy disappears “to the wires.” Chapter 26 said the wires turn it into heat at the rate \(I^2R\). Now there is a current to integrate.

Step 1 — the energy the battery delivers. The battery moves the whole charge \(Q_\text{max} = C\mathcal{E}\) through its EMF: \(U_\text{battery} = Q_\text{max}\mathcal{E} = C\mathcal{E}^2\).

Step 2 — the energy stored. From Chapter 25, \(U_C = \tfrac{1}{2}C\mathcal{E}^2\).

Step 3 — the energy dissipated in \(R\). Sum \(P = I^2R\) over the whole charge, using \(I = I_0e^{-t/\tau}\):

\[U_R = \int_0^\infty I^2R\,dt = \frac{\mathcal{E}^2}{R}\int_0^\infty e^{-2t/RC}\,dt = \frac{\mathcal{E}^2}{R}\cdot\frac{RC}{2}\]

\[\boxed{\;U_R = \tfrac{1}{2}C\mathcal{E}^2 = U_C\;}\]

The battery delivers \(C\mathcal{E}^2\); exactly half is stored and half is heat.

Check what cancelled. \(R\) dropped out of the answer. A smaller resistance carries a larger current for a shorter time, and the two effects cancel exactly: the loss is half the energy whatever \(R\) is — even for the “ideal” wires of Chapter 25’s charge-sharing problem. That is why that half could not be avoided by using better wire.

*Personal note: No matter how small you make \(R\), you still lose half the energy to heat. The only way to improve efficiency is to use an inductor instead of a resistor to limit the current — a topic for Chapter 31.

27.5 — Household Circuits and Electrical Safety

Household outlets are wired in parallel across the 120 V supply, so every device gets the full voltage — §27.2’s shared \(\Delta V\) — and the currents add at the breaker panel:

\[I_\text{total} = \frac{P_1}{\Delta V} + \frac{P_2}{\Delta V} + \cdots\]

A circuit breaker (15 A or 20 A) opens the circuit if \(I_\text{total}\) exceeds the safe limit. A 120 V, 15 A circuit can supply at most \(P_\text{max} = (120)(15) = 1800\) W.

Example: Why the Breaker Trips

A 1500 W space heater and a 1300 W microwave are plugged into the same 15 A circuit. Each draws its own current at 120 V: \(1500/120 = 12.5\) A and \(1300/120 = 10.8\) A. In parallel the currents add:

\[\boxed{\;I_\text{total} = 23.3\ \text{A} > 15\ \text{A} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{the breaker trips}\;}\]

Chapter 26’s space heater drew 15.0 A on its own — already at the limit of a 15 A circuit. The parallel rule is why a second appliance on the same circuit is the one that trips it: adding a branch lowers \(R_\text{eq}\) and raises the total current.

A short circuit is a near-zero-resistance path across the supply. The current is limited only by the wiring’s own small resistance, so it is enormous, and so is the heat; the breaker protects the wiring from fire. A ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) compares the current in the hot and neutral wires and trips in milliseconds if they differ by as little as 5 mA — current is leaking through an unintended path, possibly a person. The breaker protects the wiring; the GFCI protects you.

*Personal note: Both devices apply Kirchhoff’s junction rule to fault conditions. The breaker monitors total current; the GFCI monitors the difference between hot and neutral. Same physics, different failure modes.

27.6 — Measuring Instruments

An ammeter measures current and is placed in series, so the current it measures passes through it. It must have very low resistance (\(R_A \approx 0\)), or inserting it would reduce the current it is trying to measure.

A voltmeter measures potential difference and is placed in parallel, across the two points of interest. It must have very high resistance (\(R_V \to \infty\)), or it would draw current and change the voltage it is trying to measure.

No real instrument is ideal. The ideal ammeter is a perfect wire and the ideal voltmeter a perfect open circuit; every real instrument sits somewhere between, and slightly perturbs the circuit it measures.

Check what a voltmeter can and cannot see.

  • Across a resistor \(R\): the voltmeter is a second branch in parallel, so the combination is \(RR_V/(R + R_V)\). That is close to \(R\) — and the reading close to true — only when \(R_V \gg R\).
  • Across a battery with nothing else connected: a high-resistance voltmeter draws almost no current, so \(Ir \approx 0\) and it reads \(\approx \mathcal{E}\). A voltmeter alone cannot detect internal resistance — the aged battery of §27.1 reads nearly 12 V on the bench and 7.2 V under load.

27.7 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. EMF and terminal voltage: a real battery is an EMF \(\mathcal{E}\) in series with internal resistance \(r\); \(\Delta V_\text{term} = \mathcal{E} - Ir\), less than \(\mathcal{E}\) whenever current flows out of it.

  2. Series resistors share one current, so their voltages add: \(R_\text{eq} = \sum R_i\), larger than the largest.

  3. Parallel resistors share one voltage, so their currents add: \(1/R_\text{eq} = \sum 1/R_i\), smaller than the smallest. The rules are the reverse of the capacitor rules because \(\Delta V = IR\) and \(\Delta V = Q/C\) are built the opposite way round.

  4. Junction rule: \(\sum I_\text{in} = \sum I_\text{out}\) — charge conservation.

  5. Loop rule: \(\sum \Delta V = 0\) — potential is single-valued. A negative answer means only that the current flows opposite to the assumed direction. A battery driven backwards is being charged, and its terminal voltage exceeds its EMF.

  6. RC circuits: \(\tau = RC\). Charging: \(q = Q_\text{max}(1 - e^{-t/\tau})\), \(I = I_0e^{-t/\tau}\). Discharging: \(q = Q_0e^{-t/\tau}\). Reaching 90% or falling to 10% both take \(t = \tau\ln 10 = 2.30\tau\).

  7. The 50% result: charging a capacitor through any resistance dissipates exactly half the battery’s energy in that resistance.

  8. Ammeters go in series with low resistance; voltmeters in parallel with high resistance. Both perturb the circuit they measure.

Key Equations

Quantity Equation
Real battery \(I = \mathcal{E}/(R + r)\), \(\ \Delta V_\text{term} = \mathcal{E} - Ir\)
Power budget \(I\mathcal{E} = I^2R + I^2r\)
Series resistance \(R_\text{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots\)
Parallel resistance \(1/R_\text{eq} = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + \cdots\)
Junction rule \(\sum I_\text{in} = \sum I_\text{out}\)
Loop rule \(\sum \Delta V = 0\)
RC charging \(q = C\mathcal{E}(1 - e^{-t/RC})\), \(\ I = (\mathcal{E}/R)\,e^{-t/RC}\)
RC discharging \(q = Q_0\,e^{-t/RC}\), \(\ I = (Q_0/RC)\,e^{-t/RC}\)
Time constant \(\tau = RC\)
Time to a fraction \(t = \tau\ln(1/f)\) for \(e^{-t/\tau} = f\)
Energy in RC charging \(U_\text{battery} = C\mathcal{E}^2\), \(\ U_C = U_R = \tfrac12 C\mathcal{E}^2\)

\(P = I^2R\) Power budget \(I\mathcal{E} = I^2R + I^2r\); \(U_R = \int I^2R\,dt\)

Looking Ahead

Chapter 28 enters new territory: magnetic fields and magnetic forces. Moving charges not only respond to electric fields but also create and respond to magnetic fields. The force on a moving charge in a magnetic field, \(\vec{F} = q\vec{v} \times \vec{B}\), is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction of motion without changing the speed. This leads to circular orbits, the force on current-carrying wires, and ultimately to electric motors.

*With Kirchhoff’s rules, we can analyze any circuit in steady state. But the most interesting phenomena in electromagnetism arise when things change — when currents vary, when charges accelerate, when fields evolve in time. The magnetic field is our gateway to that richer, dynamic world.
